caption:
Grok Bot users say their weekly usage ran out days early, one at 100% with four days to go.
Asked on X if usage could be reset, Elon Musk said the cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.
He gave no numbers and did not say if limits will change.

Would you pay more for an AI agent that never runs out?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Tesla North, Anadolu Agency
threads_text: Grok Bot users burned through their weekly usage days early, and Elon Musk's reply was that serving it cost too much compared to revenue. AI agents that work in the background are expensive to run, and someone has to pay. Would you pay more for an agent with no limits?

paragraphs.text: Elon Musk said on November 1, 2026 that the cost of serving Grok Bot, the AI agent from his company xAI, had been unsustainably high relative to revenue. He made the remark on X in reply to a user who asked whether Grok Bot usage could be reset, according to Tesla North and Anadolu Agency.

The exchange followed complaints from subscribers who said their weekly Grok Bot allowance ran out much earlier than expected. One user said usage reached 100% with four days left before the weekly reset, Tesla North reported.
What Musk did and did not say

Musk did not share figures on operating costs or revenue and did not say whether the usage limits would change, according to Anadolu Agency. Tesla North noted that his use of the past tense suggests a deliberate change rather than a technical glitch, though he did not say what changed, whether plan prices will move or whether affected users will receive a reset.

A review by explainx.ai found no official xAI announcement of a cut to the weekly limits, and said the size of the allowance has not been published. It also found no announcement of a shutdown or a price increase.

xAI launched Grok Bot in early beta in August 2026. It is an agent that carries out multi-step tasks across applications inside its own virtual computer environment and can keep working in the background without active supervision. It is offered through several paid subscription tiers under the SuperGrok and Cursor brands, with usage counted separately from other allowances.

Tasks such as research, writing and web browsing use far more computing power than a simple chat reply, and that computing is what the usage limits measure, according to Tesla North. Explainx.ai reported that Grok Bot bills for the work the agent does, including tool calls, browser use and subagents, rather than per message, and that a routine scheduled every few minutes can run about 100 times a day.

Individual users have posted detailed accounts of the drain. One subscriber on the Ultra plan reported reaching 65% of the weekly allowance on the first day, 84% on the second and 99% on the third, according to explainx.ai, which said these reports could not be independently verified.

The episode shows the economic pressure behind agent products. A chatbot answers a message and stops, but an agent that browses, calls tools and runs on a schedule can consume large amounts of computing for a single request. Musk's comment is a rare public admission from an AI company leader that a flat subscription did not cover what heavy users were spending, and it suggests that limits or pricing for such agents may keep shifting across the industry.
The next signal to watch is whether xAI publishes the size of the Grok Bot allowance or changes the prices of its SuperGrok plans.
